svg.title: The four design techniques: fault isolation, information hiding, modularity and hierarchy
svg.desc: Each technique is shown with what it does, the mechanism that implements it, and what you observe when it is working. All four buy a bounded blast radius and all four cost more design decisions up front.
svg.text: Four techniques, one purpose: keep a failure inside its own box
These are the only techniques the guide names, and every later chapter is an application of one of them
1 · Fault isolation
A failure in one module or layer does not spread to the others.
HOW module boundaries, summarisation edges, separate IGP areas, redundant paths that fail independently
YOU SEE IT one area flaps, the rest keeps forwarding without a topology change
2 · Information hiding
Propagate state, not detail — every prefix you advertise is a failure you import.
HOW route summarisation, area design, hierarchy that hides the inside of a region from the outside
YOU SEE IT a leak inside one region appears to the rest of the network as a single flapping prefix
3 · Modularity
Each functional module is designed, changed and operated by a named owner.
HOW campus, data centre, WAN and edge as separate modules with explicit interfaces between them
YOU SEE IT a data-centre change is reviewed by the DC team only, and the campus team never notices
4 · Hierarchy
Core, distribution and access, each with one job and a stated responsibility.
HOW policy at the layer boundary, capacity added where it is needed, summarisation at the distribution
YOU SEE IT the diagram explains itself and a capacity question has one obvious place to go
All four buy the same thing — a bounded blast radius: the difference between "a switch died" and "the region died".
All four cost the same thing — more design decisions before the first cable is pulled, and more to explain to whoever inherits it.
None of them is free at runtime either: every boundary is a place where a route can be summarised wrongly, or a policy applied twice.
